newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish biker murder trial to open heavily guarded.
newsitem.headline: Danish biker murder trial to open heavily guarded.

text.p: Protected by the tightest security measures ever seen at a Danish court, six members or allies of the Hell's Angels bike gang go on trial on Monday accused of killing a rival in a March 10 airport shootout.

The shooting turned a festering vendetta between the Hell's Angels and the Bandidos gang into full-blooded war in which the rivals have blasted each other with machine-guns, hand grenades, bombs and anti-tank missiles across the Nordic region.

Watched by armed police, those able to show legitimate cause to attend the hearing will pass through a metal detector and be screened by officers familiar with the gangs, who will weed out known bikers with criminal records.
"There will also be uniformed police in the courtroom itself," police inspector Erik Doessing told the Danish daily Berlingske Tidende on Sunday.

Streets around the building will be closed to traffic, court officials -- including the three judges -- will be issued with security badges to be worn at all times and police bomb experts and their dogs will sweep the court before each session.
Cleaning staff have been specially vetted and will be watched by police as they work.
"The trial is taking place under the toughest security arrangements seen so far," the Politiken daily wrote.

Such precautions are new and shocking to Denmark. Before the Hell's Angels and Bandidos started fighting three years ago, street crime more often than not meant someone riding their bicycle on the pavement.
The biker feud claimed its first life in February 1994, when a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight with Bandidos in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The president of the Swedish Bandidos was killed by a sniper the following year under circumstances which make it unclear whether he was slain by a rival gang or a dissident within his own group. Police have never charged anyone with the killing.

Finnish Bandido leader Jarkko Kokko was fatally shot on a Helsinki street in March 1996, allegedly by a member of MC Finland, a gang which was seeking incorporation into Hell's Angels. Their application was granted the day after he died.
On March 10, gunmen shot dead Danish Bandidos leader Uffe Larsen and wounded three of his companions as they waited to meet fellow-members returning from a visit to Helsinki.
At almost the same time, in Norway, an attacker shot and wounded a Bandido arriving at Oslo's Fornebu airport. Police arrested a member of a Hell's Angels-allied gang.
Since then the weapons used have become heavier, three more people have died and others have been maimed.

In the trial beginning on Monday the prosecution will seek to prove that the six accused, two Hell's Angels members and two associates, jointly planned the Copenhagen airport attack and are all guilty of Larsen's murder and the attempted murder of the other three, regardless of who pulled a trigger.
"We shall prove that the six went to the airport to kill somebody," prosecutor Birgit Stamp told Politiken.
The trial, expected to take up to six weeks, is complicated by the silence of witnesses.

Bystanders are terrified to give evidence for fear of reprisals, while those within the biker fraternity are bound by a code forbidding cooperation with the police. Even the surviving victims refuse to identify their attackers.
